title: Why Your Streak Died at 20% (It Was Never Willpower)
youtube_description:
Why your streak died at 20%: the endowed progress effect, explained with two car-wash cards: 34% finished the card that already had two stamps on it, 19% finished the identical blank card.

In 2006, Joseph Nunes and Xavier Drèze handed out car-wash loyalty cards at random. One group got a blank eight-stamp card. The other got a ten-stamp card with two stamps already applied. Both needed exactly eight more washes for the same free wash. 34% of the endowed group finished; 19% of the blank-card group did. They named it the endowed progress effect: what moves people is not the work left, it is whether the task reads as not yet begun or already under way.

Then the film turns to the deadline most of us were handed. "21 days to form a habit" is not a habit finding at all. It comes from Maxwell Maltz's 1960 Psycho-Cybernetics, where a plastic surgeon wrote that patients took a minimum of about 21 days to get used to a changed face — and the word minimum went missing. When Phillippa Lally and colleagues measured habit formation in 2010 (96 volunteers, twelve weeks, one small daily behaviour each), time to feeling automatic ran from 18 days to 254, median 66. The range is the useful part: you are not late, and you were never on a clock.

The catch is the last third of the film. The endowed progress effect disappeared when no reason was given for the head start. Two squares filled in for no reason is a lie you can see, and you will not fall for your own. So the move is not to credit yourself two stamps — it is to find a reason the person you are would accept. Start the draft at the second sentence. Start the book at page twenty.

No habit-formation shortcut in 21 days. No promise that this makes you consistent. Just the one lever the research supports: decide where the card starts.

SOURCES
Nunes & Drèze (2006), Journal of Consumer Research 32(4), 504–512. doi:10.1086/500480
Kivetz, Urminsky & Zheng (2006), Journal of Marketing Research 43(1), 39–58. doi:10.1509/jmkr.43.1.39
Lally, van Jaarsveld, Potts & Wardle (2010), European Journal of Social Psychology 40(6), 998–1009. doi:10.1002/ejsp.674
Maltz (1960), Psycho-Cybernetics

Chapters
00:00 Two Cards | Same Eight Washes
00:22 One | The Twenty-One-Day Lie
00:55 Two | What They Actually Measured
01:29 Three | The Catch

Tell me in the comments what your honest reason was — that part is the whole trick, and it is the part no video can hand you.

Music: "Where Stars Fall" by Scott Buckley (CC BY 4.0).

pinned_comment:
The detail that surprised me most while researching this: the "21 days" rule has no habit study behind it. It came from a plastic surgeon in 1960 describing how long his patients took to adjust to a new face — and he wrote "a minimum of about 21 days." The word minimum is the one that got dropped.

If you try the two-free-stamps idea: what was your honest reason? Reply with it — the reason is the whole trick, and I read these.
topic: Endowed progress: why a task that looks already started gets finished, and why the 21-day habit rule has no research behind it
summary: Two people need the same eight car washes; one is handed a card with two stamps already on it and completes it 34% of the time against 19%. The film traces the endowed progress effect, exposes the 21-day habit rule as a surgeon's dropped qualifier, and hands the mechanism to the viewer: pick a start that is already in progress.
key_angle: The start of a task decides its finish. Perceived progress, not willpower, and not the size of the remaining task, is what moves people to continue.

creative._note: Written during production from this film's script, render report and inspected master frames. Weaknesses are recorded, not scored away. No analytics exist here: every audience claim is [P].

hook_candidates.text: Two people need eight car washes. One of them is already twenty percent done.
hook_candidates.why: The concrete asymmetry is the whole argument in eleven words: an identical task, an unequal start. It withholds the result (the 34 vs 19 split arrives at 00:09 as the first escalation) and it is verbatim the film's first two voiced lines, so the record does not promise an opening the film lacks.

hook_candidates.text: A car wash handed out two kinds of card. The lazier card won.
You did not quit because you were weak. You quit because your card started at zero.
Thirty four percent finished one card. Nineteen percent finished the other. Same card.

retention_map.purpose: state the unfairness before explaining it — two identical tasks, one head start, on screen as two countable cards
the cards fill to 2/10 against 0/8 and the viewer does the arithmetic themselves; the numbers land later as confirmation, not as a surprise
from a car wash to the viewer's own abandoned attempts — 'you quit because your card started at zero'
the 21-day rule is demolished; the film kills the deadline the viewer has been failing against
18 to 254 days with a median of 66 — the range removes the clock instead of replacing it with a different number
the mechanism flips from explanation to instruction: hand yourself two stamps
the catch — the effect needed a reason, so the cheap version of the idea dies here and the honest one is set up
the transferable move: start the draft at the second sentence, the book at page twenty
the opening two cards return, now nearly full, so the ending re-frames the first frame

title_candidates.why: Puts the viewer's own failure in the first clause — 'your streak' is theirs — and removes the blame in the second, which is what the film actually argues. The parenthesis carries the twist; the topic is the first half.

script_critique.revision: The first draft ran the car-wash study, the 21-day myth and the Lally data as three consecutive evidence blocks around 00:30, which is a lecture rather than a film. The 21-day debunk was moved to 00:22 and turned into a reversal against the viewer's own deadline, and the 'reframe' line ('you quit because your card started at zero') was pulled forward from the end into S03 to re-stake the promise mid-film. Retention is still the weakest criterion: the middle third is evidence, and evidence is the part a viewer can leave during.
